tracks.narration: Your program thinks it owns gigabytes of memory. In reality, only the pages you actively touch live in RAM. The rest sit on disk until you need them.
Physical memory holds a handful of page frames. The disk swap area holds many more. The present bit in each page-table entry says which store to look in.

When the CPU reads a virtual page whose present bit is zero, the hardware traps into the kernel. The page-fault handler finds the page on disk and copies it into a free frame. Then the access can be retried.
If RAM is already full, one of the resident pages has to leave first. The replacement policy picks a victim, writes it back if dirty, and only then the new page can land.
Hit in RAM, it's nanoseconds. Miss to disk, it's milliseconds. Demand paging only pays that price for what you actually use.
